catalog_quote: Dhimba, like Herero and Ndonga, is a tone language. Taking into account that the Herero and Ndonga tonemic systems have not yet been thoroughly analysed, any comparative data might not be reliable. However, there is no doubt that Dhimba employs the three level system (high, middle, low tone) like Herero does while Ndonga operates only with two tonwmic [sic] levels (Fivaz 1986:12). On the other hand, there is a tendency in Dhimba to favour high tone on terminals (personal observation) which can also be observed in urban Herero.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dhimba/Zemba is described as a lexical tone language with three tone levels (H, M, L), like Herero; the author adds an impressionistic tendency for word-final ('terminal') syllables to carry high tone. No statement about word stress or accent placement is made anywhere in the sketch, and no other opened source addresses Dhimba prosody.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only qualification is that Herero/Ndonga tonemics 'have not yet been thoroughly analysed' and the terminal-H tendency is flagged as 'personal observation'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone; 'terminals' = word-final syllables (the same term Ohly uses for verb-final vowels elsewhere in the sketch). Elderkin 2003 (p. 581) separately notes, without data, that northern Herero-related varieties may be developing a rightward-shifted 'tonal accent system' under Ndonga/Kwanyama-type influence; that remark is hedged ('I do not know to what extent') and not specific to Dhimba.
new_statements.identity_note: Ohly 1995 describes Dhimba as spoken in Namibia (Otjovanatje and Etoto in the former Owamboland/Omusati corner, Ehombo in Kaokoland, plus Opuwo/Okangwati/Ondangwa townships), self-designation Dhimba, Herero exonym Zemba -- i.e. zemb1238 [dhm] itself, not Himba or standard Herero (here1253). Data were collected by J.U. Kavari's team (Kaokoland 1987/88) and J.Z. Kuvare's team (Owamboland 1988/89). Angolan Dhimba is not covered by Ohly; Cameron & Kunkel 2002 cover both countries but only sociolinguistically.

sources.locator: section 'Comparative data: Tone', pp. 8-9 (PDF pp. 4-5); verified against the page images
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. 'Phonetics' and 'Tone' sections (pp. 8-9): Dhimba is a tone language with a three-level system (H, M, L) like Herero, vs two levels in Ndonga; 'a tendency in Dhimba to favour high tone on terminals (personal observation)'. Rest of the 48-pp sketch is noun-class/verb morphology, morphophonemics and lexicostatistics vs Herero and Ndonga; the only 'stress' tokens are the English verb 'to stress'.

sources.note: Nothing; vitality survey plus an 83-word spelling comparison OluZemba/Otjiherero/Oshiwambo; explicitly defers 'phonological and syntactic analysis' to future work (p. 43).

sources.citation: Elderkin, Edward D. 2003. Herero (R31). In D. Nurse & G. Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 581-608. London: Routledge.
sources.note: Describes standard (southern) Herero only: two tones H/L plus 'tone keys'; no word stress statement. Sec. 1 (p. 581) explicitly excludes the northern Herero-related varieties (Kaoko/Angola, i.e. Himba/Dhimba area): 'I do not know to what extent the Herero-related varieties north of the Etosha Pan have been influenced by tonal systems similar to those of Ndonga (R22) and Kwanyama (R21), in which high tone seems to have moved to the right and a tonal accent system may be developing; the tonal system described here relates to the southern (standard) variety.'

sources.note: Nothing; recorded-text intelligibility testing (Herero/Ndonga), language use and literacy questionnaires in Namibia and Angola; no linguistic description, no wordlist with prosodic marking.
